title: Gluten-Free Alcohol: A Celiac-Safe Guide to Beer, Wine and Spirits
excerpt: Which alcohol is gluten-free? A celiac-friendly guide to spirits, wine, cider, hard seltzer, and gluten-free beer, plus why gluten-reduced beer and bar mixers need care.
metaDescription: Which alcohol is gluten-free? A celiac guide to vodka, whiskey, wine, cider, seltzer and gluten-free beer, plus the drinks and bar mixers to avoid.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most alcohol is either naturally gluten-free or treated as gluten-free by the major celiac organizations. Wine, cider, hard seltzer made from cane sugar, 100% agave tequila, rum, brandy, and plain distilled spirits like vodka, gin, and whiskey are generally safe for people with celiac disease. The big exception is **regular beer**, which is brewed from barley (and often wheat) and contains gluten. The tricky middle ground is **"gluten-reduced" beer** and **flavored drinks with added ingredients**, where you need to read labels carefully. This guide walks through each type of drink, explains why distilled spirits made from wheat can still be gluten-free, and gives you a practical shopping and ordering list.

**The quick list:**

- **Generally gluten-free:** wine, sparkling wine, most hard cider, cane-sugar-based hard seltzers, 100% agave tequila and mezcal, unflavored rum, brandy and cognac, unflavored vodka (including grain vodka), gin, and straight whiskey.
- **Contains gluten:** regular beer, ale, lager, stout, porter, and malt liquor; most flavored malt beverages like Smirnoff Ice and Twisted Tea.
- **Check the label:** "gluten-reduced" or "crafted to remove gluten" beers, flavored spirits and liqueurs, pre-mixed cocktails, ciders made by breweries, and anything with beer or malt added.

> **This is not medical advice.** If you have celiac disease, a wheat allergy, or non-celiac gluten sensitivity, your own doctor or a registered dietitian who specializes in celiac disease is the best guide to what you can safely drink. People react differently, and some people with celiac disease choose to avoid even products that celiac groups consider safe. **See a doctor if** you keep having digestive symptoms, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or rashes after drinking even though you're avoiding gluten, or if you notice blood in your stool. **Call 911** if you have a wheat allergy and develop hives, swelling of the lips or throat, trouble breathing, or dizziness after a drink.

## What Makes a Drink Contain Gluten?

Gluten is a group of proteins found in **wheat, barley, and rye** (and close relatives like spelt and triticale). In people with celiac disease, gluten triggers an immune reaction that damages the lining of the small intestine. Even small amounts eaten regularly can keep that damage going, which is why "a little bit" matters so much for people with celiac disease.

Alcohol gets gluten in one of three ways:

1. **It's fermented from a gluten grain and not distilled.** This is beer. Barley is malted, mashed, and fermented, and gluten proteins stay in the finished drink.
2. **Gluten gets added after the main process.** Think flavorings, colorings, malt additives, or a splash of beer in a cocktail.
3. **Cross-contact.** A cider made on the same equipment as beer, a shared tap line at a bar, or a glass that last held beer.

Drinks made entirely from naturally gluten-free ingredients (grapes, apples, sugarcane, agave, potatoes, corn, rice, sorghum) and kept away from gluten along the way are gluten-free from the start.

## Why Distilled Spirits Are Considered Gluten-Free (Even From Wheat)

This is the question that confuses most people. How can a vodka made from wheat, or a whiskey made partly from barley and rye, be gluten-free?

The answer is **distillation**. To make a spirit, producers first make a fermented liquid (a kind of rough beer or wine), then heat it. Alcohol and some flavor compounds turn to vapor at lower temperatures than water, rise, and are collected as they cool. Gluten proteins are large, heavy molecules that don't vaporize, so they stay behind in the leftover liquid in the still. The clear liquid that comes out the other end doesn't carry the gluten with it.

That's why major celiac organizations in the US, including the **Celiac Disease Foundation** and **Beyond Celiac**, consider pure distilled spirits gluten-free regardless of the grain they started with. Coeliac UK takes the same position.

There are two honest caveats:

- **Additives after distillation.** Once a spirit is distilled, producers can add flavorings, colorings, sweeteners, or other ingredients. Plain spirits rarely contain anything gluten-based, but flavored vodkas, spiced rums, cream liqueurs, and some whiskey "finishes" are worth checking.
- **Some people still react.** A number of people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity say they feel unwell after grain-based spirits and do better with spirits made from gluten-free sources like potatoes, grapes, corn, or agave. There's no good evidence that gluten survives distillation, but if you notice a pattern, switching to a naturally gluten-free spirit costs you nothing. It's your body and your call.

## Beer: The Main Thing to Avoid

Regular beer is the one alcoholic drink that clearly contains gluten. That includes lagers, ales, IPAs, stouts, porters, wheat beers, and malt liquor. "Light" beers are still brewed from barley malt, so they aren't gluten-free either. Neither are most non-alcoholic beers, which start as regular beer before the alcohol is removed.

Fortunately, there are two kinds of beer-like options for people avoiding gluten, and they are **not** the same thing.

### True gluten-free beer

True gluten-free beer is brewed from grains that never contained gluten: **sorghum, rice, millet, buckwheat, corn, or gluten-free oats**. Because there was never any gluten in the recipe, these beers can legally be labeled "gluten-free" in the US.

Brands that have built their names on this include **Redbridge** (a sorghum beer from Anheuser-Busch), **Glutenberg** (a dedicated gluten-free brewery in Montreal), **Ghostfish Brewing** in Seattle, and **Holidaily Brewing** in Colorado. Availability varies a lot by region, so check what your local stores carry. Dedicated gluten-free breweries are the safest choice because there's no barley in the building to cause cross-contact.

Expect a different taste. Sorghum beers in particular have a slightly tart or fruity edge. Many newer gluten-free brewers use millet and rice to get closer to a classic lager or pale ale flavor.

### "Gluten-reduced" or "gluten-removed" beer

These beers are brewed from barley like normal beer, then treated with an enzyme that breaks gluten proteins into smaller pieces. **Omission** is the best-known example. They often taste just like regular beer, which is the appeal.

The problem is testing. Standard gluten tests are designed to find whole gluten proteins. Once the enzyme chops gluten into fragments, those tests may not reliably measure what's left, and small lab studies have found that fragments from some gluten-reduced beers can still react with antibodies from people with celiac disease. Whether those fragments cause intestinal damage in real people isn't settled.

Because of that uncertainty, US labeling rules don't allow these beers to say "gluten-free." They can say something like "crafted to remove gluten," along with a statement that the gluten content can't be verified and the beer may contain gluten. The Celiac Disease Foundation and Beyond Celiac both advise people with celiac disease not to rely on gluten-removed beers. If you have celiac disease, treat them as **not gluten-free**. Some people with milder gluten sensitivity do drink them, but that's a personal decision best made with your doctor.

## Wine and Sparkling Wine

Wine is made from fermented grapes, so it's naturally gluten-free. Champagne, prosecco, cava, and other sparkling wines are too.

You may read online about two possible gluten sources in wine:

- **Fining agents.** Winemakers sometimes use a substance to clear haze out of wine before bottling. Wheat gluten has been used for this in the past, but it's uncommon, and most fining agents are things like bentonite clay, egg whites, or gelatin.
- **Barrel sealing.** Some oak barrels have historically been sealed with a wheat flour paste.

Testing reported by gluten-free advocacy groups has found that any gluten getting into wine this way is very low, generally below the 20 parts per million threshold the FDA uses for a "gluten-free" label. Celiac organizations consider regular wine safe.

The places to be careful are **wine coolers** and **flavored wine drinks**. Some are made with malt beverage bases rather than wine, and they can contain barley. Read the label before assuming a wine-style drink is safe.

If wine tends to give you a headache, that's almost certainly not gluten. Our guides to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) and [sulfites in wine](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) explain the more likely culprits.

## Hard Cider

Cider is fermented from apples (or pears, for perry), so it's naturally gluten-free, and many major cider brands label themselves gluten-free.

Two things to watch for:

- **Brewery-made ciders.** A cider produced by a beer brewery may run on shared equipment. Look for a gluten-free statement on the label or the maker's website.
- **Added ingredients.** Some specialty ciders add barley malt, beer yeast blends, or flavorings. "Beer-cider hybrids" obviously contain gluten.

As a rule, a cider that says "gluten-free" on the can or bottle is a safe bet.

## Hard Seltzer and Ready-to-Drink Cans

This category is where label reading matters most, because two cans can look nearly identical and be made in completely different ways.

**Most big-name hard seltzers** are made from a fermented cane sugar base, not malt. White Claw and Truly, for example, both describe their seltzers as gluten-free. Brand recipes can change, so a quick label check is still worth it.

**Flavored malt beverages** are a different story. Drinks like **Smirnoff Ice** (in the US) and **Twisted Tea** are made from a malt base, which means barley. Despite the vodka branding on some of them, they are not the same as a vodka soda, and they aren't a safe default for someone with celiac disease.

**Canned cocktails** made with real spirits (vodka sodas, gin and tonics, margaritas) are usually gluten-free, but check the ingredients list for malt, natural flavors from unclear sources, or a "contains wheat" allergen statement.

For more on why seltzers can still leave you rough, see our [hard seltzer hangover guide](/never-hungover/hard-seltzer-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

## Spirits, One by One

Here's how the main spirits stack up. "Plain" means unflavored, with no added ingredients.

| Spirit | Usual base | Gluten status (plain) | What to watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vodka | Wheat, rye, corn, potato, grapes | Gluten-free (distilled) | Flavored vodkas. Potato, corn, and grape vodkas suit people who prefer to avoid grain-based spirits. Tito's (corn) labels itself gluten-free. |
| Gin | Usually grain, flavored with juniper and botanicals | Gluten-free (distilled) | Botanicals are added during or before distillation, so plain gin is fine. Check sweetened or flavored gins. |
| Whiskey / bourbon / Scotch | Barley, corn, rye, wheat | Gluten-free (distilled), per celiac groups | Cask finishes, flavored whiskeys, and whiskey liqueurs. Some people prefer to avoid it and choose another spirit. |
| Tequila / mezcal | Agave | Gluten-free | Choose "100% agave." Cheaper "mixto" tequilas can be made with up to 49% other sugars and may contain additives. |
| Rum | Sugarcane or molasses | Gluten-free | Spiced and flavored rums, which can contain added flavorings. |
| Brandy / cognac | Grapes or other fruit | Gluten-free | Flavored brandies. |
| Liqueurs | Varies widely | Varies | The biggest gray area. Cream liqueurs, some herbal liqueurs, and anything flavored can contain added ingredients. Check the maker's allergen information. |
| Sake | Rice and koji mold | Generally considered gluten-free | Some sakes add distilled alcohol or flavorings. Ask or check the label if you're sensitive. |

If you like vodka, gin, or tequila, our guides to [vodka hangovers](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), [whiskey hangovers](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), and the [truth about tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) cover how each one tends to affect the next morning.

## What the Labels Actually Mean in the US

Alcohol labeling in the US is split between two agencies, which is why the rules can feel inconsistent.

- **The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB)** oversees most spirits, wine at 7% alcohol or above, and beer made from malted barley and hops.
- **The FDA** oversees wine under 7% alcohol and beers not made from both malted barley and hops, which includes many sorghum-based gluten-free beers.

Both follow the same basic idea:

- **"Gluten-free"** can go on products made from ingredients that don't contain gluten and handled so they meet the FDA's limit of fewer than 20 parts per million of gluten.
- **Products made from gluten grains but processed to remove gluten** (like gluten-reduced beer) can't simply say "gluten-free." They have to use wording like "processed to remove gluten" or "crafted to remove gluten," with a note that the gluten content can't be verified.

One more thing to know: alcohol isn't required to carry a full ingredients list in the US, so a missing gluten statement doesn't tell you much either way. When in doubt, check the producer's website or contact them. Many brands answer allergen questions directly.

## Hidden Gluten at the Bar

Even when your drink starts out safe, a few common habits can add gluten:

- **Beer in the cocktail.** Micheladas, shandies, beer-based punches, and "boilermakers" all contain beer.
- **Bloody Mary mixes.** Some contain malt vinegar or a Worcestershire sauce made with malt vinegar. Ask what mix the bar uses, or order a simple vodka soda instead.
- **Malt-based mixers.** Some ready-made sour mixes and flavored syrups contain barley malt or malt extract.
- **Shared taps and glassware.** Cider poured from a line that recently ran beer, or a glass that wasn't cleaned well, can pick up traces.
- **Garnishes.** Beer-battered snacks or rim salts mixed with seasonings aren't the drink itself, but they end up in your mouth along with it.

The simplest safe orders when you're unsure: a glass of wine, a plain spirit with soda water and fresh citrus, a margarita made with 100% agave tequila and fresh lime, or a can of cider or seltzer that says "gluten-free."

## Celiac Disease, Gluten Sensitivity, and Wheat Allergy Aren't the Same

These three conditions get lumped together, but they affect what you can drink in slightly different ways.

- **Celiac disease** is an autoimmune condition. The goal is to avoid gluten strictly, because even small repeated exposures can damage the intestine without obvious symptoms. Follow the celiac organizations' guidance: distilled spirits, wine, and cider are generally fine; regular and gluten-reduced beer are not.
- **Non-celiac gluten sensitivity** causes symptoms like bloating, fatigue, or brain fog after eating gluten, without the intestinal damage of celiac disease. Tolerance varies a lot from person to person.
- **Wheat allergy** is an allergic reaction to wheat proteins, which can be severe. It's a different immune pathway from celiac disease, and allergists don't all give the same advice about wheat-based spirits. If you have a wheat allergy, ask your allergist which drinks are safe for you before experimenting.

## Does Gluten-Free Alcohol Mean a Better Morning?

Switching to gluten-free drinks won't change how much alcohol you're drinking, and alcohol is what drives a hangover. A gluten-free beer has about as much alcohol as a regular one, and a vodka soda is still a shot of vodka.

That said, some people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity notice that drinking gluten makes their next day much worse, with bloating, digestive upset, and fatigue on top of the usual hangover. For them, choosing gluten-free options can make a real difference to how they feel, even if it's the gluten reaction rather than the hangover itself that improves.

Drink type matters a bit too. Darker drinks tend to contain more **congeners**, the flavor by-products of fermentation and aging, and some research has linked higher-congener drinks to worse hangovers. Our [congeners guide](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains this, and our [beer hangover guide](/never-hungover/beer-hangover) covers why beer can hit some people harder than they expect.

The habits that help most are the same for everyone: eat a real meal before drinking, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, pace yourself, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through what has the best evidence.

## A Note on Supplements If You Avoid Gluten

Some people also use supplements around drinking. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people, so treat it as an add-on to good habits, not a replacement for drinking less.

If you avoid gluten, apply the same rule to supplements that you apply to drinks: **check the label for a gluten-free statement, or contact the maker before you buy.** Capsule fillers and coatings occasionally use wheat-derived ingredients. If you'd like to try DHM, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Confirm the current allergen information on the listing or with the brand before you order. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## When to See a Doctor

Most people who ask about gluten-free alcohol already know they need to avoid gluten. But it's worth seeing a doctor if:

- You get bloating, diarrhea, stomach pain, or fatigue after eating or drinking gluten and **haven't been tested for celiac disease**. Testing works best while you're still eating gluten, so talk to a doctor before cutting it out completely.
- You have celiac disease and **still have symptoms** even though you're carefully avoiding gluten, including in drinks. A dietitian can help track down hidden sources.
- You notice **blood in your stool, unexplained weight loss, or ongoing anemia**. These need a proper check-up regardless of the cause.
- You have a **wheat allergy** and aren't sure which drinks are safe. An allergist can give advice specific to you.

**Call 911** if anyone has signs of a serious allergic reaction after a drink: swelling of the face, lips, or throat, trouble breathing, widespread hives, or feeling faint.

## The Bottom Line

- **Safe for most people avoiding gluten:** wine, sparkling wine, hard cider labeled gluten-free, cane-sugar hard seltzers, and plain distilled spirits, including vodka, gin, whiskey, rum, brandy, and 100% agave tequila.
- **Avoid if you have celiac disease:** regular beer, most non-alcoholic beer, flavored malt beverages, and "gluten-reduced" beer.
- **Read the label on:** flavored spirits, liqueurs, canned cocktails, brewery-made ciders, and wine coolers.
- **Watch for hidden gluten at the bar:** beer-based cocktails, some Bloody Mary mixes, and shared taps.
- Gluten-free alcohol is still alcohol. Pacing, food, and water do more for the next morning than any drink swap.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What alcohol is gluten-free?**

Wine, sparkling wine, most hard cider, cane-sugar-based hard seltzers, 100% agave tequila, unflavored rum, brandy, and plain distilled spirits like vodka, gin, and whiskey are generally considered gluten-free. Regular beer contains gluten, and so do most flavored malt beverages. Flavored spirits, liqueurs, and canned cocktails vary, so check the label or the maker's website.

**Is vodka gluten-free if it's made from wheat?**

Yes, according to major celiac organizations such as the Celiac Disease Foundation and Beyond Celiac. Distillation leaves gluten proteins behind in the still, so plain distilled vodka is considered gluten-free whatever grain it started from. Flavored vodkas can have added ingredients, and some people prefer potato, corn, or grape vodka if they notice a reaction to grain-based spirits.

**Is whiskey safe for people with celiac disease?**

Plain distilled whiskey, including bourbon and Scotch, is considered gluten-free by celiac organizations because distillation removes gluten proteins. Flavored whiskeys, whiskey liqueurs, and some cask-finished products can contain added ingredients. A minority of people with celiac disease say they react to whiskey anyway; if that's you, switching to a spirit made from a gluten-free source is an easy fix.

**Is there gluten-free beer?**

Yes. True gluten-free beer is brewed from grains that never contained gluten, such as sorghum, rice, millet, or buckwheat, and can be labeled gluten-free in the US. Examples include Redbridge and beers from dedicated gluten-free breweries like Glutenberg, Ghostfish, and Holidaily. This is different from gluten-reduced beer, which starts with barley.

**Is gluten-reduced beer like Omission safe for celiacs?**

Celiac organizations advise people with celiac disease not to rely on it. Gluten-reduced beers are brewed from barley and treated with an enzyme that breaks gluten into fragments, but standard tests may not reliably measure those fragments, and small lab studies have found some can still react with antibodies from people with celiac disease. US rules don't allow these beers to be labeled gluten-free.

**Are hard seltzers gluten-free?**

Most major hard seltzers, such as White Claw and Truly, are made from a fermented cane sugar base and are described as gluten-free. Flavored malt beverages like Smirnoff Ice and Twisted Tea are a different category: they're made from a malt base containing barley and are not gluten-free. Always check the can, because similar-looking drinks can be made in different ways.

**Is wine gluten-free?**

Yes. Wine and sparkling wine are made from grapes and are naturally gluten-free. Wheat-based fining agents and flour-sealed barrels are rare, and celiac organizations consider regular wine safe. Be careful with wine coolers and flavored wine drinks, which can be made from a malt base.

**Is cider gluten-free?**

Cider is made from apples and is naturally gluten-free, and many cider brands label their products gluten-free. Watch for ciders made in breweries on shared equipment, beer-cider hybrids, and specialty ciders with added malt. A gluten-free statement on the label is the simplest check.

**Will gluten-free alcohol give me a lighter hangover?**

Not by itself. Hangovers are driven mainly by how much alcohol you drink, and gluten-free drinks contain just as much alcohol. People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may feel noticeably better the next day if they avoid gluten, because they skip the digestive reaction. Pacing, eating beforehand, and drinking water help everyone more than any drink swap.
